Composer and trumpeter Ambrose Akinmusire’s honey from a winter stone was released January 31, 2025, on Nonesuch Records. The album, which Ambrose calls a “self-portrait,” features improvisational vocalist Kokayi, pianist Sam Harris, Chiquitamagic on synthesizer, drummer Justin Brown, and the Mivos Quartet (violinist Olivia Deprato and Maya Bennardo, violist Victor Lowrie Tafoya, cellist Tyler Borden). Akinmusire says, “In many respects this entire work is inspired by and is an homage to the work of the composer Julius Eastman and his organic music concept."

“This album is about the fears and struggles I personally face, as well as those many Black men endure: colorism, erasure, and the question of who gets to speak for my community, and why,” Akinmusire explains. “There’s also the constant negotiation of what happens when I don’t conform to certain expectations or when I choose to reject those imposed on me. These are the complexities I navigate daily.”

“When I made this album, I was thinking about others who face these same struggles,” he continues. “I’m always considering who I represent—on all levels, in all the roles I play within my various communities. It’s about understanding the weight of those roles and the responsibility that comes with them.”

The Jewel in the Lotus is the debut album by jazz woodwind player Bennie Maupin, recorded in March 1974 and released on ECM Records. It features a sextet with Herbie Hancock on acoustic and electric pianos, Buster Williams on bass, Billy Hart and Freddie Waits on drums, and Bill Summers on percussion. Charles Sullivan makes guest appearances on trumpet. The album's title is a translation of the Buddhist mantra "Om Mani Padme Hum". The music is described as deep, meditative, and spiritual, with influences from jazz-fusion, avant-garde jazz, and modal jazz. The album has been widely acclaimed as a jazz classic, noted for its rich soundscapes and the interplay of the musicians.

Another Time: The Hilversum Concert is a never-before-issued live recording by the Bill Evans Trio, featuring pianist Bill Evans, bassist Eddie Gomez, and drummer Jack DeJohnette. It was recorded at the Netherlands Radio Union (NRU) VARA Studio 8 in Hilversum, Holland, on June 22, 1968, and officially released by Resonance Records on September 1, 2017. This album is notable for being only the third known recording of this specific trio, which was active for a six-month period in 1968. The recording is praised for its exceptional sound quality, captured using the then state-of-the-art equipment of the NRU, and preserved in pristine condition over the years. This release followed the success of 'Some Other Time: The Lost Session from the Black Forest', which was recorded just two days prior to 'The Hilversum Concert'.

Easy Walker is an album by jazz saxophonist Stanley Turrentine, released in February 1968 on the Blue Note label. The album features Turrentine alongside a versatile quartet including McCoy Tyner on piano, Bob Cranshaw on bass, and Mickey Roker on drums for the initial tracks. The recording sessions took place at Van Gelder Studio in Englewood Cliffs, NJ, with tracks recorded across multiple dates in July 1966, July 1967, and June 1969 for bonus tracks on later reissues.

The album is known for its soulful tenor saxophone sound and engaging hard-grooving numbers, alongside sultry ballads. It includes an interpretation of Burt Bacharach and Hal David’s “What The World Needs Now Is Love” and the album opener “Meat Wave.” Critics, such as Stephen Thomas Erlewine of Allmusic, describe it as a good, relaxing soul-jazz session that allows the musicians to work a good groove and showcase their improvisational skills. The album was produced by Alfred Lion for tracks 1-7 and Francis Wolff for tracks 8-11.

Ella and Louis Again is a studio album by Ella Fitzgerald and Louis Armstrong, released in October 1957 on Verve Records. It serves as the sequel to their 1956 collaboration, Ella and Louis. This album deviates from its predecessor by featuring seven solo vocal tracks by either Armstrong or Fitzgerald alongside its twelve duet tracks. The album was recorded at Radio Recorders and Capitol Studios in Hollywood. It was later reissued as part of a two-compact disc set in 1995 and included in The Complete Ella Fitzgerald & Louis Armstrong on Verve in 1997.

Interplay is a 1963 studio album by American jazz pianist Bill Evans. Recorded in July 1962 in New York City, the album was originally released by Riverside Records. It features a quintet lineup, with Evans on piano, Freddie Hubbard on trumpet, Jim Hall on guitar, Percy Heath on bass, and Philly Joe Jones on drums. This recording is notable for showcasing Evans in a quintet setting, departing from his more common trio format, and it helped establish him as a formidable bandleader. The album comprises a selection of jazz standards alongside the Bill Evans original title track. The recording sessions were produced by Orrin Keepnews.

Following in the footsteps of 2022’s Return from the Stars, which found saxophonist Mark Turner gazing past the horizon of earthly jazz into a more cosmic register, his quartet with trumpeter Jason Palmer, bassist Joe Martin, and drummer Jonathan Pinson returns with the aptly titled Patternmaster. If its predecessor charted a voyage outward, this record feels like the mapping of constellations discovered along the way. Lines weave and bob with adroit precision while maintaining a pliant freedom that lets the occasional jab of surprise land with force. Turner and Palmer operate as simpatico melodic leads, their phrases joining and separating like a quasar whose pulse cannot be predicted but somehow feels inevitable. Turner has long been a paragon of control in tone, technical craft, and compositional balance. Yet something in these performances carries the gravity of accumulated time. The music speaks with an elder’s clarity without surrendering its curiosity. One hears not only mastery but also a widening orbit of possibility. The album’s title reaches outward into literature through the first book of science fiction writer Octavia E. Butler’s Patternist series, a saga in which telepaths form intricate networks of shared consciousness. Butler imagined communities linked by invisible threads of perception, individuals whose thoughts reverberate through an unseen lattice of awareness. Her fiction often asked difficult questions about power, responsibility, and the fragile architectures that bind societies together. Turner’s quartet mirrors that speculative vision through sound. Each musician senses the others before the note fully arrives, improvisation functioning as a kind of musical telepathy. Melodies propagate through the ensemble like signals traveling through Butler’s imagined psychic web. Turner also gestures toward Wayne Shorter, whose own compositions often seemed to arise from dimensions beyond surface-level perception. In that lineage, Patternmaster proposes jazz as a field of relational intelligence. Ideas migrate from instrument to instrument, forming configurations that only exist because several minds are listening at once.

Rigmor Gustafsson is without a doubt one of Sweden’s most successful jazz singers of all time. She studied in New York in the 90s where she formed her own band and has been touring worldwide since then. The trio's remarkable interplay—developed over decades of collaboration—creates a conversational approach to improvisation that feels both intimate and expansive.

The compositions reflect a sense of unease about the challenges facing humanity, yet they also carry an undercurrent of hope. Shaped in close collaboration with the band members, equally internationally respected musicians Adam Forkelid, Calle Rasmusson, and Tuulikki Bartosik, the arrangements reveal a shared musical vision that adds depth and vibrancy to the narrative. In these pieces, music becomes a form of resilience, a reminder that creativity and imagination still hold power, even against all odds.

"New Standards, Vol. 1" is a bold reimagining of what constitutes the jazz canon, led by master drummer, vocalist, and producer Terri Lyne Carrington. Released in 2023 on Candid Records, this album challenges traditional notions of the "Great American Songbook" by presenting contemporary compositions as worthy successors to the classic standards.

Carrington, a three-time Grammy winner and the founder of the Berklee Institute of Jazz and Gender Justice, brings together an exceptional ensemble of musicians for this project. The band features pianist Kris Davis, whose angular harmonic approach provides fresh perspectives on the material; bassist Linda May Han Oh, whose compositional voice and supportive yet adventurous playing anchor the group; trumpeter Nicholas Payton, adding his distinctive voice and genre-defying approach; and guitarist Matthew Stevens, whose contemporary sound palette expands the ensemble's sonic possibilities.

The album's repertoire includes works by contemporary composers and artists across various genres, treating songs by Esperanza Spalding, Robert Glasper, and others with the same reverence traditionally reserved for Gershwin and Porter. This conceptual framework suggests that today's generation deserves their own standards—songs that speak to contemporary experiences and sensibilities while maintaining the artistic depth and emotional resonance of the classics.

Carrington's drumming throughout is a masterclass in supportive yet dynamic playing, propelling the music forward while leaving ample space for her bandmates to express themselves. Her occasional vocals add an intimate dimension to certain tracks, demonstrating her multifaceted artistry beyond the drum kit.

"New Standards, Vol. 1" is more than just an album—it's a statement about the evolution of jazz repertoire and a celebration of the rich compositional voices of the 21st century. By positioning contemporary works as new standards, Carrington opens up conversations about canonization, tradition, and the future of the music, all while delivering performances of remarkable beauty and sophistication.

Armenian piano virtuoso Tigran Hamasyan's latest album Manifeste is a powerful fusion of jazz, progressive rock, and Armenian folk. Recorded across five countries between 2023 and 2025, the album blends rhythmic complexity, cinematic depth, and spiritual intensity, featuring longtime collaborators and the Yerevan State Chamber Choir. Manifeste explores themes of seeking, transformation, and creative renewal, unfolding as a ritual-like sequence from meditative pieces to powerful anthems. Hamasyan integrates Armenian folk and sacred sources with jazz improvisation, rock-derived rhythmic language, and compositions for solo piano, ensemble, and choir. The album is described as a bold declaration where the human, digital, and sacred unite in sound, showcasing Hamasyan's fascination with transcendence and transformation.

The recording features an all-star lineup of musicians who navigate the challenging charts with remarkable cohesion and individual brilliance, anchored throughout by McBride's powerful, virtuosic bass playing.

Trilogy 3 is a live album by Chick Corea and his trio, featuring Corea on piano with Christian McBride on double bass and Brian Blade on drums. This three-disc album brings together live performances from their February-March 2020 tour, which was cut short by the onset of the pandemic. The album showcases their unparalleled chemistry and artistic brilliance, featuring fresh interpretations of jazz standards and Chick Corea originals, including the first trio recording of Corea's iconic composition 'Windows' since its appearance on the album Now He Sings, Now He Sobs, nearly six decades ago. It marks another milestone for this celebrated ensemble, following the critically acclaimed Trilogy (2013) and Trilogy 2 (2018) albums, both of which earned Grammy Awards.

Ellas Kapell's fourth album, 'Ember,' is a bold step into modern vocal jazz. Known for their emotionally charged interpretations of standards, the Swedish quartet expands their sonic landscape. The album is self-produced, showcasing a new level of artistic control and blending acoustic and electronic elements.

Released on February 27th, 2026, via Naxos Prophone, 'Ember' reimagines jazz standards such as 'Very Early' and 'All the Things You Are.' The group, featuring vocalist Lovisa Jennervall, Manne Skafvenstedt (piano, synths), August Eriksson (double and electric bass, violin), and Edvin Glänte (drums, percussion), delivers intimate yet expansive music. Additional instrumentation includes Johan Christoffersson (alto sax), Tobias Wiklund (cornet), and Gustav Alte (pedal steel). The album balances jazz tradition with fresh creative heat, inviting new audiences beyond the traditional jazz sphere.

The title 'Moder' (Mother) reflects a caring force that delves into both an earthly connection and a more abstract, overarching theme.

Released on Warner Music on April 3, 2026, Kind of Now - The Pulse of Miles Davis is drummer and composer Gregory Hutchinson's tribute project marking the centennial of Miles Davis. Rather than recreating Davis's recordings, the album extends the conversation Davis began, with Hutchinson framing the project as a continuation of that lineage.

The ensemble pairs Hutchinson on drums with trumpeter Ambrose Akinmusire, tenor saxophonist and bass clarinetist Ron Blake, pianist Gerald Clayton, guitarists Jakob Bro and Emmanuel Michael, and bassist Joe Sanders. The program spans compositions by Miles Davis, Wayne Shorter, Tony Williams, and three Hutchinson originals, drawn from different periods of Davis's discography.

Hutchinson, who also produced the record, uses distinct tonal colors and cymbal choices as compositional tools across the session. The album incorporates trio settings, fusion-leaning passages, and three solo drum tracks, totaling roughly 57 minutes of music.

What Day Is It is the debut LP from Fonville x Fribush, released February 27, 2026 via WarHen Records. The 10-track album was cut live over two days at Minimum Wage Recording in Richmond, Virginia, part of a session that yielded more than 30 takes in total.

The trio is drummer Corey Fonville (Butcher Brown), organist Sam Fribush, and guitarist Alan Good Parker, who also contributes pedal steel. Sam Fribush's 1962 Hammond B3 organ anchored the sessions; the studio's owner reportedly had to remove a door to fit the instrument into the tracking room.

The record was produced by Corey Fonville and Sam Fribush, recorded and mixed by Lance Koehler at Minimum Wage Recording, and mastered by Rob Dobson at Hear Garden in Los Angeles. WarHen Records issued the album on Blue Chips vinyl (limited to 125 copies) and Classic Black vinyl (limited to 200 copies), alongside a digital release.

What Day Is It is the debut LP from Fonville x Fribush, released February 27, 2026 via WarHen Records. The 10-track album was cut live over two days at Minimum Wage Recording in Richmond, Virginia, part of a session that yielded more than 30 takes in total.

The trio is drummer Corey Fonville (Butcher Brown), organist Sam Fribush, and guitarist Alan Good Parker, who also contributes pedal steel. Sam Fribush’s 1962 Hammond B3 organ anchored the sessions; the studio’s owner reportedly had to remove a door to fit the instrument into the tracking room.

The record was produced by Corey Fonville and Sam Fribush, recorded and mixed by Lance Koehler at Minimum Wage Recording, and mastered by Rob Dobson at Hear Garden in Los Angeles. WarHen Records issued the album on Blue Chips vinyl (limited to 125 copies) and Classic Black vinyl (limited to 200 copies), alongside a digital release.
